reason: The sources provide multi-site corroboration for Mercury's 88-day orbit, 59-day rotation, Colombo's 3:2 resonance, and radar observations across independent platforms.
story: For nearly a century, astronomers were certain that Mercury was tidally locked to the Sun, dragging one face through perpetual daylight and the other through frozen night. Because its orbital year was 88 Earth days, mapmakers assumed its rotation was identical. But in the 1960s, scientists bounced radar beams off Mercury and measured an unexpected spin rate of roughly 59 days. Italian mathematician Giuseppe Colombo cracked the mystery: Mercury wasn't locked 1:1, but in a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance, completing three axial rotations for every two orbits around the Sun. Because of this cosmic geometry, a single solar day from sunrise to sunrise on Mercury lasts 176 Earth days—precisely two full Mercury years. The myth had survived so long simply because whenever Mercury was best placed for telescopic observation from Earth, the orbital geometry happened to reveal the exact same side.
angle: Astronomers spent a century convinced Mercury kept one face frozen and one face fried, until radar revealed it rotates three times every two orbits—making one day last two entire years.

claims.claim: Astronomers long believed Mercury was tidally locked to the Sun with an 88-day rotation period matching its orbital period.
Mercury takes approximately 88 Earth days to complete one orbital revolution around the Sun.
Mercury's actual rotational period is approximately 59 Earth days.
Italian celestial mechanics specialist Giuseppe Colombo proposed that Mercury rotates once every 59 Earth days instead of 88 days.
Radar techniques were developed and used to measure Mercury's spin rate from Earth.
A single solar day from sunrise to sunrise on Mercury lasts approximately 176 Earth days, or two Mercurian years.
Surface temperatures on Mercury reach extreme highs exceeding 700 Kelvin (over 400 degrees Celsius).
Mercury has an extremely tenuous atmosphere that is properly classified as a surface-bounded exosphere.
Permanently shadowed craters at Mercury's poles harbor water ice detectable by radar reflections.
NASA's Mariner 10 mission performed three flybys of Mercury across 1974 and 1975.
Mariner 10's flybys mapped less than half (about 45%) of Mercury's surface.
Mercury possesses a dipolar magnetic field roughly 1% the strength of Earth's magnetic field.
Observations confirm that Mercury possesses a fluid, molten metallic core.
As Mercury's interior cooled and shrank, its surface buckled into thrust fault cliffs and scarps hundreds of kilometers long.
NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft launched in 2004 and achieved orbit around Mercury in 2011.
The Caloris Basin is a massive impact basin on Mercury measuring approximately 1,500 to 1,550 kilometers across.

disputed: Volcanic plains vs. impact melt: Lunar geologists debated for decades whether Mercury's smooth plains were caused by volcanic lava flows or impact ejecta; a script should attribute this as an ongoing scientific debate that MESSENGER helped clarify with volcanic vent evidence.

Crustal thickness measurements: Mariner 10 and MESSENGER data indicate a thickness of about 35 km, while Airy isostasy models estimate 26 ± 11 km; a script should leave this detail out or attribute it as differing model estimates.
Cause of the 'Weird Terrain': Competing hypotheses attribute the disrupted terrain opposite Caloris Basin to focused seismic shockwaves or converging ejecta; attribute as 'theorized by scientists'.
